The incursion, which occurred in June, was not made public until last week.
In a blog post, the ChatGPT maker apologized for the hacking and acknowledged it ‌mishandled its response ⁠and ⁠pledged to take accountability to “rebuild trust with the Australian people.”

item.title: Malaysia starts sending Myanmar migrants home
item.description:
Malaysia began sending back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals Tuesday, AFP journalists saw, launching a scheme rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.
The batch is the first of 5,000 Myanmar citizens Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centers amidst a huge uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.
But advocacy organizations say dire conditions in detention centers may have forced their decisions, and they could face dangerous homecomings in Myanmar where war has raged since 2021.
Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have officially clarified the number of Rohingya in the first group, and there is concern they may be returned to a country where they face persecution rights groups say amounts to genocide.
Dozens of buses arrived under police escort on Tuesday at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia, AFP correspondents saw, where the migrants were to be processed.
They will then be transported to the nearby naval base and taken to Myanmar by ship.
A Myanmar security source, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to media, said the boats are due to dock at Thanlyin Navy Base just south of Yangon around the end of this week.
Marine traffic websites showed Myanmar’s auxiliary support and hospital ship Than Lwin at anchor just outside the naval base.
Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 members of the Rohingya.
The plan was announced after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur.
They were seeking help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state.
They were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation.
Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.
Last week more than 160 civil society groups in a joint statement called upon the Malaysian government to “immediately halt the deportations,” pending talks with civil organizations about the situation on the ground in Myanmar.
Anwar said he would invite Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-civilian president Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit to help expedite the repatriation process.
But the civil groups urged that “Malaysia’s engagement with the junta must not come at the expense of its own reputation and integrity.”
Malaysia’s home affairs ministry last month said 5,000 individuals will undergo voluntary repatriation as agreed by the Myanmar government.
There were 10,388 Myanmar nationals held at immigration detention depots by mid-August, the ministry said, with not all considered refugees.
Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognize refugee status.
AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fueling xenophobia and intimidation.
Many of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim group, escaped Myanmar during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.
Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled Myanmar after the offensive, which is the basis of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.
More than 1.2 million live just over the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, but talk of repatriations from there has yielded little progress.

item.title: Iran threatens new strikes as it awaits US response to Hormuz plan
item.description:
Iran on Tuesday threatened to attack infrastructure around the Middle East, intensifying its rhetoric as it awaits a formal response from Washington on a new plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump has already dismissed the proposal from Tehran, but Iran’s foreign minister said Monday that he was expecting a formal response from American officials in the coming day.
Fighting has subsided in recent weeks, though Tehran has continued to target ships in the strait, with Washington falling back on an economic pressure campaign instead of further military action.
Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Tuesday threatened new attacks, saying no infrastructure in the region would be safe if his country’s security was not guaranteed.
“In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either; or if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will remain safe,” Ghalibaf, who is also Iran’s parliament speaker, said according to video released by state TV.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he expected a formal answer from the US on Tuesday to Tehran’s proposal, state media reported.
Iran has maintained a blockade on commercial shipping through Hormuz since the war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic.
The shipping route carried a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the conflict began.
The US military has been maintaining a counterblockade of Iran’s ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting oil.
Araghchi said late Monday that Qatari intermediaries “presented ideas, and we discussed them; they are set to raise the matter with the American side once more, after which the final US response will be conveyed to us.”
The top diplomat, who was in New York for the UN General Assembly, said “The Qataris hope this will be done by tomorrow.”
“The current focus is solely on the Strait of Hormuz, and the reopening of the strait is contingent upon the fulfilment of certain conditions that we have communicated to the other side,” he added.
Last week, discussions were held in New York between Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
As a precondition for ending its blockade, Iran is demanding a seven-day ceasefire across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah is regularly bombarded by Israel.
It is also demanding the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade on its ports.
Both sides claim to have control of Hormuz, with the US saying oil is moving through and Tehran insisting the waterway is closed.
On Tuesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of the country’s military, said “the US claim that it remains open is false.”
“Sneaking a few hundred barrels of oil through under the cover of darkness -- with transponders turned off and at great cost -- does not constitute the strait being open,” said spokesperson Hossein Mohebi.
“A truly open strait is one where, as in the past, at least 125 vessels would pass through daily, transporting a minimum of 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum products.
“Any vessel attempting to pass through sustains damage -- either we strike it, or it hits a mine,” he added.

item.title: Building bridges: Lessons from Ta-Nehisi Coates
item.description:
“There is more wisdom in your body than in your deepest philosophy.”
Between the World & Me (Spiegel & Grau, 2015) by Ta-Nehisi Coates is a book-length exposition of racism in the United States.
True to the advice from Nietzsche above, he explores the topic not through philosophical musings but through the brutal lived experience.
Written as a letter to his son, Samori, the book is an archive of Coates’ personal life through the Black neighborhood.
Although Coates’ book is centered around his experiences growing up as a Black person in the United States, his words reflect every colonized nationality in history.
And what gets lost in the cold, dry words of history, sociology, and statistics is how much the legacy of racism still lingers on to this day.
Coates analyses how Black bodies are not their own but are still very much at the hand of their colonizers, despite how much the colonizers want to think otherwise.
He wants us to dig deeper into who the "people" are in Lincoln’s “Democracy is government by, for and of the people”?
Questioning the US’ claim of being the greatest nation on earth, Coates is skeptical whether the police who murder Black teenagers in the streets in broad daylight disproportionately truly go against the ideals of their nation. Or are they the proud progeny of the country’s history?
The US, or for that matter almost every empire on the face of the earth, has been built on blood.
Today, Israel continues to do the same with Palestinians; the only difference is this time the world has the internet to see everything. Every colonizer has a history of genocide.
That’s evident in Coates’ book when he describes his visit to Paris. He understands that being Black there is not the same as in the US, but that supposedly noble country is also built on the backs of Algerians.
All of this is to elicit the simple question: can racism be solved if only people are good at their intentions? Coates thinks the answer is "NO."
History has been unfair to the oppressed, and the unfairness continues its legacy. Black neighborhoods don’t have better schools because of being located in suburbs, which is a direct result of segregationist policies of a not-so-distant time.
The colonizers have to recognize this fact and admit that the problem is not only because of individual acts but also the history, policies and economics that remain hidden.
Admitting this can result in a broken dream, as Coates refers to continuously in his book. Most Americans and the colonizers try their hardest to avoid the question of systemic change, focusing only on “goodwill” and “good intentions."
They quote Martin Luther King Jr.’s famous speech “I Have a Dream," where he wants his children to be judged by their character, not by their skin, pointing to that as the goal.
But they conveniently leave out the fact that he also advocated systemic changes and reparations his whole life, and was hated by the racists all over the country in his time.
The US is terrified of its history. From whitewashing the narrative of Thanksgiving to anti-CRT mania, this fact has been vindicated. Similar stories have been told to justify the oppression of the natives here as well: the British were the civilizers of the savages here.
But, as promised, Coates forces us to focus on the daily effects of racism. He recalls the fear he saw in his elders, who got terrified when a child got lost while playing in the park.
He remembers his father saying, “Either I beat him or the police," which was a method of control so that children would be cautious of the world around them and not get killed.
He doesn’t want his son, Samori, to be “tough” or acquainted with the street attitude but can’t shake off the fear that one day he will lose him too, just as he lost his friend at Howard University due to police violence.
He talks about his wife and other Black women and realizes that, as whites couldn’t always bridge the gap between their world and his, similarly he couldn’t always bridge the gap between her world and his. And the bridges can only be traversed through communication and honest inquiry.
But that step is still far away for most Americans. Most of them are happy to include Black and Native people as tokens for diversity, without solving the root issue.
The recent George Floyd case can be an example. After the “Black Lives Matter” protests, many words such as police reform and diversity training were floating around.
Many corporations took a stand with this movement. But as usual, in the end, it was virtue signaling at the corporate and national level.
Keeping one or two Black mayors or a president cannot solve the historical legacy of racism. It has to take into account the legal frameworks that have disadvantaged Black people and the economic issues that have strangled them for decades.
Coates’ book is also significant to understanding how racism can be expressed subtly, which should be a lesson for everyone to be cautious while framing language.
Black History Month is a celebration of all oppressed races on the earth, every native culture that has been destroyed or lost because of imperial ambitions.
Coates searched his whole life to find a way to bridge the gap between his two worlds, how it should be and how it was.
He wants the bridge to vanish for his son so that he can live a true life on his own, in his true body, true self, in a truly free country, not a country free for one race of people.
Black History Month should be directed towards that goal so that every race and ethnicity can bridge the gap between them and their world.
Sadman Ahmed Siam is a student at the Islamic University of Technology.

item.title: Gold Over Rot
item.description:
Sometimes I want so much from God my faith stands in the doorway and refuses to let me ask. I do not ask for houses, for gold, for kingdoms, I ask for gold foil over my sins, something bright enough to hide what is rotten underneath. I ask for pride in who I am, pride in who I shall be tomorrow morning, and still I wake hungry, gluttonous with that disgusting little prayer of more, more, more, until even my hands forget what they were reaching for. Then I am angry with God for giving me nothing. Nothing, when I brought Him my hunger and called it faith, brought Him my weakness and called it fate, brought Him a heart full of wanting and wondered why it never learned how to be full.
Nubisha Rabya Topote, an XI-grade student at Holy Cross College, is a poet and writer who finds inspiration in the world around her. Find more of her work at @nubishawrites.

item.title: Adabor house takeover attempt foiled; 10 arrested
item.description:
Ten people have been arrested in a case filed over an alleged attempt to seize a house, vandalise property and extort money in Adabor, Dhaka, police said.
Four of the suspects, including two who were injured in police gunfire, were arrested during an overnight operation. Police said they opened fire in self-defence after the suspects allegedly attempted to attack officers with machetes.
The incident took place around 2:30am on Monday in an open area beside a canal behind a playground near Kacha Bazar in Naboday Housing, Adabor.
The two injured suspects were identified as Rajib Howlader, 30, and Sagar, 24. Both sustained gunshot wounds to their legs and were taken to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital for treatment.
The other two arrested during the operation were identified as Shakib, 23, and Rashed, 24.
Adabor police said they launched the operation around 2am based on information about the suspects’ whereabouts. Seven to eight people were present at the scene.
When police attempted to arrest them, the suspects allegedly tried to attack officers with machetes. Police then fired two rounds from a shotgun carried by a constable in self-defence, according to police.
Rajib and Sagar were injured, while the others fled. Police recovered numerous weapons from the scene.
Adabor police station Officer-in-Charge Zahidul Islam said police opened fire after the suspects allegedly attempted to attack them.
“The injured were sent to hospital. Legal action will be taken in connection with the incident,” he said.
The OC said six people had previously been arrested in the case, and the four arrests during the overnight operation brought the total number of suspects arrested to 10.
According to police, Sagar has eight cases filed against him with Adabor and Mohammadpur police stations. Rajib is a named accused in the Babu murder case in Mohammadpur.
Shakib and Rashed each have five cases against them, police said.
On Sunday, a group of 15-20 people allegedly attacked a house in Shyamoli Housing, Adabor, carrying machetes, ramdas and pistols, in an alleged attempt to seize the property.
A case was filed with Adabor police station over the incident.
Police said the two sides had been involved in a longstanding dispute over ownership of the house and that a court case concerning the property is ongoing.

The killing of 13-year-old Ishayat Shahriar Apratim in Comilla, who was allegedly lured from his home on the pretext of making a TikTok video, has renewed concerns over the safety of children and teenagers using social media.
Police are investigating several aspects of the case, including Apratim’s contact with older youths, an iPhone, a Tk5,000 debt and the claim that he was called out to make a TikTok video. However, investigators have yet to establish a definitive motive.
Concerns over the risks of social media use among minors are not new. In July, a 20-year-old man was arrested in Feni for allegedly recording and sharing on TikTok an incident involving the harassment of a six-year-old child. In September, a teenage girl was allegedly raped in Comilla after travelling there to meet a young man she had met through Facebook and TikTok.
These incidents cannot simply be attributed to social media. However, they illustrate how children’s and teenagers’ online interactions can have consequences for their safety in the real world.
Several countries have introduced or are considering age restrictions on social media. Australia, Indonesia and Malaysia have adopted different measures for users under 16, while the UK and others are considering similar steps.
In Australia, restrictions on people under 16 opening or maintaining accounts on specified platforms took effect on December 10, 2025. Platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Snapchat, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube are required to take “reasonable steps” to prevent under-16s from holding accounts. Children and their parents are not subject to penalties, with primary responsibility placed on the platforms.
Indonesia introduced similar restrictions in March 2026, while Malaysia introduced age-verification requirements on June 1, 2026.
Bangladesh does not currently have a specific minimum age of 16 for opening social media accounts. However, the 2026 Bangladesh Telecommunication (Amendment) Act includes provisions for technical parental controls and, where necessary, age-based verification to protect children and minors using the internet and digital devices and to prevent harassment. Detailed procedures are to be set out in regulations.
Professor Dr M Rezaul Islam of the Institute of Social Welfare and Research at the University of Dhaka said an age limit alone could not eliminate online risks.
“However, restricting children from having personal social media accounts below a certain age may protect them from some online risks. At the same time, social media platforms must be held accountable, while parents should also be given the skills and knowledge needed to ensure digital safety and awareness,” he said.
A 2025 UNICEF Bangladesh U-Report survey, which received responses from around 29,000 children and young people, found that two-thirds identified excessive fake news and misinformation on social media as the biggest source of mental stress. About one in seven cited bullying and negative comments, while a similar proportion identified harmful or upsetting content as a major concern.
The survey also found that 52% of respondents considered rules against harmful behaviour such as bullying and hate speech important, while 79% believed that relaxing such rules could put vulnerable groups at greater risk.
Bangladesh’s expanding internet access means children are increasingly growing up in connected households. The 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and UNICEF found that 72.1% of households have internet access at home.
The BBS ICT Access and Use by Households and Individuals Survey 2024–25 found that 53.4% of people in Bangladesh use the internet, including 75.7% in urban areas and 43.6% in rural areas. However, the survey does not specifically measure internet use among children.
A 2025 study published in BMJ Open , involving 456 students aged 13–18 at four schools in urban and rural Bangladesh, found that about 88% used the internet. Mobile phones were the primary means of access for 84% of respondents. The study was not nationally representative.
Globally, internet use among young people is also widespread. According to 2025 data from the International Telecommunication Union, 82% of people aged 15–24 use the internet, compared with 72% among those outside that age group.
The World Health Organization’s Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study, which analysed data from around 280,000 adolescents aged 11, 13 and 15 across 44 countries and regions, found that problematic social media use rose from 7% in 2018 to 11% in 2022. The rate was 13% among girls and 9% among boys.
Psychiatrist Dr Bulbul Ahmed Khan said adolescents may not always be able to assess the long-term consequences of communicating with strangers online, taking part in risky challenges or being exposed to harmful content in the same way as adults because parts of the brain involved in risk assessment, emotional control and decision-making are still developing.
“Therefore, children need age-appropriate protection and guidance from adults in their online experiences up to a certain age. However, simply imposing restrictions or setting an age limit will not solve the problem. Open communication within the family, digital literacy, the ability to identify online risks and mental health support when necessary all need to be ensured together,” he said.
Belayet Hossain, a resident of Azimpur, said his Class 8 child uses a phone for studies and communication, but he worries about what the child does online and who they communicate with.
“Simply taking the phone away will not solve the problem,” he said, adding that he tries to maintain open communication so his child feels comfortable telling the family if a stranger makes contact or a problem arises online.
“Social media platforms should also take children’s safety more seriously,” he added.
Another key question is how an age limit would be implemented.
Professor Dr M Rezaul Islam said requiring children to submit national identity cards, birth registration documents or other personal information to every platform could create new privacy risks.
“Therefore, alongside an age limit, Bangladesh also needs to ensure data minimisation, privacy protection and independent oversight,” he said.
Privacy has also been a key consideration in Australia, where the eSafety Commissioner says age-verification methods must comply with privacy safeguards and users are not required to provide government-issued identification.
Emerging regulatory models also place responsibility on social media platforms, rather than solely on children and their parents. This raises questions over how much responsibility platforms should bear for verifying users’ ages, filtering harmful content, preventing online grooming and protecting children’s accounts.
The government has also acknowledged concerns over harmful content on social media and the need for greater oversight.
Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam said in August that the government was working with social media companies and other stakeholders to regulate harmful content and protect young people from digital risks.
“The ICT Ministry is collaborating with social media companies and relevant stakeholders to establish proper oversight and safeguard our future generation,” he said.
Earlier in July, he told Parliament that the government was working to strengthen coordination with international technology platforms, including YouTube and TikTok, to remove harmful content. He said the government was considering amendments to the Cyber Security Act to improve the process.
China Akter, administrative officer of the Organisation-3 Branch at the Information and Communication Technology Division, said the government was working on measures to ensure a safe digital environment for children, including age-appropriate protection, parental controls and age verification.
“Setting a specific age limit alone cannot reduce online risks. Effective age-verification measures, control of harmful content and responsible practices by social media platforms are also needed,” she said.
“Children should also be made more aware of digital safety, while social media platforms should play a responsible role in creating a safer online environment for them,” she added.
Imtiaz Bin Hafiz, an executive member of Ain o Salish Kendra, said simply telling children not to use certain apps would not protect them from online risks.
“Digital platforms also benefit commercially from children’s participation and engagement. Therefore, responsibility for children’s safety should not rest solely on children and their families. Platforms must also take responsibility and ensure safety measures and child safety by design,” he said.
At the same time, social media can provide children and teenagers with opportunities for education, communication, access to information, creativity and social participation. UNICEF has also noted that digital technology can help children learn, play and communicate, while stressing the need for skills to navigate the digital world safely.
The investigation into Apratim’s killing has once again highlighted how social media can be used to contact and influence children and teenagers. However, the circumstances and motive behind his killing remain under investigation.

item.title: The curious case of 600 ‘lost’ passports a day
item.description:
Nearly 600 Bangladeshi passports are reported lost every day. But many of them may not be “lost” in the conventional sense.
Behind the extraordinary number are passports allegedly withheld by recruiting or visa agencies, documents migrant workers cannot retrieve from employers or intermediaries abroad, and cases in which passports are reported lost, or even deliberately destroyed, in connection with irregular migration, according to findings by the Department of Immigration and Passports.
The scale is striking.
Department sources say 107,300 applications citing lost passports were received in a six-month period, averaging around 17,885 a month and nearly 600 every day.
The volume has become a matter of concern for passport authorities, who are having to process the replacement applications alongside regular applications for new passports and renewals.
It has also prompted the government to tighten the rules for replacing lost, stolen or damaged passports.
While there will be no additional penalty for the first occurrence, anyone reporting a passport lost, stolen or damaged for a second or subsequent time will have to pay an additional Tk10,000 on top of the regular passport fee.
The provision came into effect on September 21 under a new government circular.
But officials say the more intriguing question is what lies behind such a large number of passports being reported lost.
Officials at the Department of Immigration and Passports acknowledge that passports are inevitably lost, stolen or accidentally damaged.
But the scale and circumstances of the applications prompted the department to examine why so many people were seeking replacements.
Officials say they identified three recurring patterns.
The first begins before a traveller even leaves Bangladesh.
Many aspiring migrant workers and travellers hand over their passports to recruiting, travel or visa agencies to process visas.
In some cases, the agencies fail to secure the promised visa but continue to hold the client’s passport while delaying the process with repeated assurances.
Unable to recover the document and desperate to move on, some passport holders eventually file a General Diary with police saying the passport has been lost and use the GD to seek a replacement, officials said.
In effect, the passport may still physically exist, but its holder no longer has access to it.
The second pattern occurs overseas.
Bangladeshi migrant workers sometimes surrender passports to employers, sponsors or agencies while residence and work permits, including iqama in some Middle Eastern countries, are processed.
Problems arise when a worker receives a better job offer or decides to change employment but cannot retrieve the passport.
According to passport officials, some then approach the relevant Bangladesh mission and report the passport lost because they see no other way to obtain a new travel document.
The government’s new rules specifically recognise situations in which a visa agency, individual or institution unlawfully withholds a passport and the holder is unable to recover it.
In such cases, the previous passport can be revoked and a replacement issued through the prescribed procedure.
The third category identified by officials is more sensitive.
Passport authorities say some cases are connected to irregular migration.
According to officials, people who enter or remain in another country through irregular channels may seek a new passport after reporting the original lost.
In some cases, they said, a passport may even be deliberately destroyed or discarded before its holder seeks another one.
The department has not provided a breakdown of the 107,300 applications showing how many fall into each of these categories.
The explanations therefore represent patterns identified by passport officials and should not be taken to mean that most or all lost-passport applications involve deliberate misrepresentation.
Nevertheless, officials say the findings help explain why the number of replacement applications has reached a level that can no longer be treated simply as a matter of people accidentally misplacing documents.
As applications continued to pile up, the Department of Immigration and Passports raised the issue with the Home Ministry during the previous interim government’s tenure.
Several meetings were subsequently held to consider how repeated passport losses could be discouraged.
Officials said policymakers were conscious that a Tk10,000 penalty would be substantial for many Bangladeshis given prevailing socio-economic conditions.
Ultimately, however, they decided against penalising someone for a first incident while imposing a significantly higher cost on repeated cases.
Under the new system, a person reporting a passport lost, stolen or damaged for the first time will pay only the regular fee required for reissuance.
From the second occurrence onwards, the applicant will have to pay an additional Tk10,000 each time.
The new rules were formalised through a government circular issued on September 21 and signed by Deputy Secretary Mohammad Nuruzzaman.
The circular also lays down a more structured procedure for dealing with lost, stolen and damaged passports.
A passport holder must immediately report the incident through the designated online system of the Department of Immigration and Passports and simultaneously file a General Diary at the nearest police station.
Police will then have 72 hours to verify the GD and submit a report.
If no police verification report is received within that period, the applicant can proceed with the reissuance process by submitting a copy of the GD, after which a “Lost Circular” will be initiated.
The procedure is intended not only to facilitate replacement but also to ensure that a passport reported missing is quickly identified within immigration and law-enforcement systems.
Information on a lost or stolen passport will be entered into the Special Branch’s Immigration Management System immediately after the report is received.
INTERPOL may also be informed where necessary.
The circular separately addresses one of the problems identified during the department’s investigation, passports being withheld by third parties.
If a visa agency, individual or institution unlawfully keeps someone’s passport and efforts to retrieve it fail, the holder can seek revocation of the original document and issuance of a new passport.
This means passport holders in such circumstances will have a formal route to seek replacement rather than continuing indefinitely without access to their travel document.
Bangladeshis who lose their passports overseas must report the matter to the relevant Bangladesh embassy, high commission or other diplomatic mission.
The mission will issue the necessary Lost Circular and process the application for reissuance.
Replacement will not completely erase the history of the missing document.
The data page of a passport reissued following a reported loss will state: “Previous Passport is Reported to be Lost.”
Applicants will also not be able to use the reissuance process to change fundamental identity information such as their name, parents’ names or date of birth.
That provision is intended to ensure continuity between the identity attached to the cancelled passport and the replacement document.
The new rules also address what happens when someone finds a passport after already reporting it lost.
Once the original passport has been revoked, recovering it does not make it valid again.
The holder cannot use the recovered passport for international travel and must notify the relevant authorities or police so that the document can be dealt with according to procedure.
The restriction is significant because a passport reported lost or stolen may already have been entered into immigration databases as an invalid travel document.
ATM Abu Asad, additional director general for passport, visa and immigration at the Department of Immigration and Passports, said the volume of applications involving lost, stolen or damaged passports had become a concern.
“We have issued certain guidelines to raise awareness among passport holders,” he told Bangla Tribune.
“We have not imposed any additional fee for the first instance,” he said.
“However, an extra Tk10,000 has been set as a penalty for a second occurrence. This measure is intended solely to foster awareness.”
The department’s message, he said, was ultimately about responsibility.
“Our appeal is for passport holders to be responsible and keep their passports safe.”
Yet the department’s own examination suggests that responsibility is only part of the story.
Some passports really are lost. Some are stolen or damaged. Others, according to officials, remain in the hands of agencies or employers their owners can no longer reach.
And some become entangled in the much murkier world of irregular migration.
Together, they have produced an extraordinary statistic: around 600 Bangladeshi passports reported “lost” every day.

item.title: New DCs appointed in four districts
item.description:
The government has appointed new deputy commissioners (DCs) to four districts — Tangail, Nilphamari, Patuakhali and Pirojpur.
The Public Administration Ministry issued a notification on Tuesday, announcing the appointments.
According to the notification, Pirojpur Deputy Commissioner Abu Sayied has been transferred and appointed DC of Tangail.
Ministry of Public Administration Deputy Secretary Md Golam Rabbani has been appointed DC of Pirojpur.
Meanwhile, Deputy Secretary of the Finance Division Md Humayun Kabir has been appointed DC of Nilphamari, while fellow Finance Division Deputy Secretary Chowdhury Ashraful Karim has been appointed DC of Patuakhali.

item.title: Salahuddin: No decision yet on how caretaker govt will be formed
item.description:
No decision has yet been taken on the process or composition of the caretaker government, Home Minister and chairman of the Special Committee on Constitutional Amendments Salahuddin Ahmed said on Tuesday.
He made the remarks at a press conference at the National Parliament Media Centre after the committee’s fourth meeting.
“An open discussion is needed on the caretaker government system, its process and the form of its formation. We need proposals. Parliament will consider what is deemed appropriate and we will accept it,” Salahuddin Ahmed said.
“We have not yet been able to decide what process to follow or who will be included in forming the caretaker government,” he added.
The committee sought the views of media professionals involved in electronic media, television channels, online portals, news management and television talk shows, Salahuddin said.
He said the committee had held discussions with editors, senior journalists and representatives of journalists’ organizations on Sunday and continued the consultations over two days as a single day was not sufficient to hear everyone’s views.
He urged participants who had made proposals or recommendations to submit them in writing. Some have already done so, while others are expected to submit theirs, he said.
“Today’s meeting involved many important discussions, and we received many valuable opinions. Some of them are significant and can be considered. We will discuss them at the committee meeting,” he said.
The written submissions will be reviewed together once they are received, he said, adding that the committee would gradually consult all groups and individuals it plans to engage.
Salahuddin said the committee would consult people from different professions and walks of life, prominent citizens, constitutional experts, lawyers, serving and former judges, academics, and various social forces, organizations and individuals associated with the July uprising.
The committee will also meet people and their families who, according to him, suffered deprivation over the past 17 years, as well as families of those killed in the July uprising.
He said the committee would seek to understand the views and recommendations of people from different professions and their representatives before consulting prominent constitutional experts and preparing a report.
Asked about a meeting with the National Consensus Commission, Salahuddin said the committee would also consult those who contributed to the drafting of the July National Charter.
The meeting also heard proposals on whether Bangladesh needs a bicameral parliament, Salahuddin said.
“One proposal was whether Bangladesh needs a bicameral parliament at all. Since this is a unitary state and has a unitary government, they said the matter could be considered,” he said.
He said the committee intended to proceed on the basis of the agreement to establish a bicameral parliament in the July National Charter.
“Since we agreed in the July National Charter that we will form a bicameral parliament, we want to proceed on that basis. But they have made a proposal. If that proposal is considered by Parliament, and if the ruling party considers it, then it can be discussed,” he said.
The meeting also discussed the decentralization of the judiciary, judicial independence and the caretaker government system, he said.
Salahuddin said the committee wanted detailed proposals on the caretaker government system and the process for forming it.
“An open discussion is needed on the caretaker government system, its process and the form of its formation. We need proposals,” he said.
He said the July National Charter contained some proposals on the issue, with notes of dissent in some areas. The committee wanted views on which of the first, second, third or fourth steps should be followed in forming the caretaker government, he said.
“Alternative proposals are needed on this issue. We need everyone’s opinions. Parliament will consider the proposal that we deem appropriate for the nation, and we will accept it,” he said.
The committee also received differing views on the proposal to limit an individual’s tenure as prime minister to a maximum of 10 years, Salahuddin said.
Some participants argued that setting a 10-year limit would be undemocratic and contrary to democratic rights. Others said that if a prime minister performs well and the people want them to serve again, they should be able to do so, he said.
Salahuddin, however, said his party’s position remained unchanged.
“We proposed this during the drafting of the July National Charter on behalf of our party. Our honourable chairman had not become prime minister at that time; he made the proposal. We made it in accordance with the decision of the Standing Board. We then mentioned it again in our election manifesto,” he said.
“We have not moved from our position. If the opposition makes any proposal in Parliament, that can be discussed then,” he added.
The committee also discussed engaging with the opposition, Salahuddin said.
“We discuss with the opposition. Our discussions are open. Through you, I urge them to nominate their representatives to the Constitutional Amendment Committee, join it and participate in the discussions,” he said.
He also urged those who had submitted proposals to participate in the discussions.
The committee aims to bring about constitutional amendments through a participatory and inclusive process after consulting all stakeholders, he said.
Asked about several of the 11 reform commission reports not being discussed by the National Consensus Commission, Salahuddin said the government was committed to implementing the July National Charter as it had been formulated.
He said the July National Charter was based on the reports of six reform commissions: the Constitutional Reform Commission, Electoral Reform Commission, Judicial Reform Commission, Administrative Reform Commission, Anti-Corruption Commission Reform Commission and Police Reform Commission.
Almost all political parties had held discussions with these reform commissions, after which their reports were used to seek further views and the National Consensus Commission was formed, he said.
The reports of the remaining reform commissions were not brought into that process, he said, adding that the government could form new, subject-specific reform commissions to seek public recommendations if necessary.
“The government can form reform commissions on various issues and seek reports. For example, if we now think of forming a Media Reform Commission, the government can do so at any time. If its recommendations are implementable, they can be implemented,” he said.
Salahuddin said the committee would consult constitutional experts after gathering views from people from different professions and walks of life.
“We will then prepare the report based on their advice. After that, we will present the report to Parliament, on the basis of which a bill will have to be placed before the National Parliament. There will then be further discussion in Parliament and outside it,” he said.
He expressed hope that the process would lead to an acceptable set of constitutional amendments.
Committee members and Chief Whip of Parliament Nurul Islam Moni; Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Home Affairs Zainul Abedin; State Minister for Planning Md Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki; State Minister for Expatriates’ Welfare Md Nurul Haque; State Minister for Land Mir Mohammed Helal Uddin; State Minister for Social Welfare Farzana Sharmin; and committee member Md Mahmudul Hoque Rubel attended the meeting.
Representatives of various electronic, television and online media outlets, as well as participants in television talk shows, were also present.

item.title: River erosion takes serious turn in Gopalganj, Satkhira
item.description:
River erosion at three points along the Shaildah River in Tungipara upazila of Gopalganj is threatening the 3-km Lebutala-Dumuria Road, disrupting travel for around 30,000 people in 10 villages.
Around 1,200 metres of the riverbank at Sarabari, Chithalia and Chhoto Dumuria in Dumuria union have been affected by erosion. Water Development Board (WDB) is dumping sandbags as a temporary measure, while locals are demanding permanent protection.
Several sections of the road have already collapsed, forcing residents to take 9-10km detours. Around 50 homes, farmland, a water supply tank, schools and religious institutions are also at risk.
“River erosion has already washed away my home and land. Now the road is also disappearing,” said Mohammad Shamim Molla, 60, of Sarabari.
Some van drivers said parts of the road have collapsed or sunk, making it difficult to operate vehicles. “In some places, we have to ask passengers to get off. Tyres get punctured, chains break, and bearings and motors are damaged,” one of them said.
College student Hridoy Sheikh said 3,000-4,000 people use the road daily, but ambulances, fire service vehicles and other large vehicles can no longer access some sections. “If permanent protection is not provided immediately, the road will disappear into the river,” he said.
WDB Sub-Divisional Engineer Mohammad Zakaria Ferdous said erosion was occurring along a 1,200-metre stretch at three points. “We are dumping sandbags as a temporary measure. A permanent riverbank protection project is being taken up under the South East Project,” he said, adding that the project would help prevent further erosion.
Meanwhile, a 50-metre section of Water Development Board (WDB) embankment in Ashashuni upazila of Satkhira has collapsed, putting 12 villages at risk of flooding. The erosion occurred in the Sripur-Kurikahunia area of Pratapnagar union.
Locals said water could enter residential areas if the breach is not repaired immediately, potentially flooding Pratapnagar and neighbouring areas. Part of the WAPDA road alongside the embankment has also collapsed, making the route risky for commuters.
Residents began emergency repair work on a voluntary basis, dumping sand and soil along the damaged section.
Abdul Khaleq, a resident of Kurikahunia village, said locals live in constant fear of flooding. “We have to struggle with the river throughout the year. Just as our homes, trees and crops begin to recover, we face another threat of flooding,” he said, adding that thousands of fish enclosures could be washed away.
Nur-e-Alam Siddiqui, a resident of Sripur, said that if this section completely collapses, Pratapnagar and neighbouring Anulia union could also be inundated. “We urgently need the WDB to intervene,” he added.
Ashashuni Upazila Nirbahi Officer Shyamananda Kundu said he had asked the local union chairman to begin preliminary repair work and informed WDB. “WDB will start work soon,” he said.
Abdur Rahman Tazkia, executive engineer of WDB Satkhira Division-2, said, “About 50 metres of the embankment has been damaged. We will start work as soon as possible,” he said.
Meanwhile, locals continue working voluntarily to prevent the erosion from worsening. They fear that without swift action, the breach could expand and cause widespread damage to homes, farmland and fish enclosures.

item.title: Humaiun: Hasina has no chance of returning to Bangladesh
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir has said former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has no chance of returning to Bangladesh, describing her planned virtual participation in an event in London as a “meaningless activity.”
He made the remarks while responding to reporters after a meeting with South Korean Ambassador Kim Ji-jun at the Foreign Ministry on Tuesday.
Asked about the government’s position on Hasina and her son Sajeeb Wazed Joy joining a news conference in London virtually on Wednesday, Kobir said the event was not being organised by the UK government. He said the government would inform the relevant authorities if necessary.
“Speaking virtually from India to an event in London, these are meaningless activities,” he said.
On Hasina’s political future, Kobir said, “There is no opportunity for her to return to Bangladesh. Those who flee or are driven out have very little chance of returning.”
Kobir also criticised Hasina’s 15-year rule, alleging that she had “persecuted” people and damaged various state institutions. He further alleged that her family members and party leaders were involved in looting the country.
“Those who fled or were driven out, their politics is over. That is where it ends,” he said.
The government has previously said it is pursuing diplomatic and legal efforts to bring Hasina back from India.

item.title: Rising feed ingredient costs threaten poultry industry
item.description:
A sharp price hike in essential feed raw materials has pushed Bangladesh’s poultry industry into severe distress.
Over the last month alone, costs for crucial feed ingredients—including corn, de-oiled rice bran (DORB), rice bran, and soybean meal—have escalated sharply.
Md Ramzan, a poultry retailer at Central Road in the capital, said: "I sold broiler chicken at Tk200 per kg on Wednesday, but with feed prices continuing to rise, wholesale costs will inevitably force us to raise prices further in the coming days."
Since raw materials account for 80% to 85% of total poultry feed production costs, this surge has heavily inflated manufacturing overheads, threatening farmers, supply chains, and consumer food affordability nationwide.

Several overlapping global, domestic, and macroeconomic forces have created a perfect storm for the feed industry:
Industry impact
Unable to absorb mounting production costs, many small and marginal farmers are downsizing operations or facing outright closure.
Over the past four months (June to September), frustrated farmers across Rajshahi, Gazipur, Pabna, Narsingdi, and Dhaka staged demonstrations, human chains, and road blockades demanding lower feed prices, reduced import tariffs, and fair pricing for livestock products.
The macroeconomic consequences extend directly to the broader economy.
Feed mills cannot sustain long-term operations on credit or maintain 6-month raw material reserves without draining capital.
Since feed drives poultry and egg production costs, retail prices for animal protein are climbing. As supply shrinks due to farm closures, chicken and egg prices risk spiking further, fueling general food inflation.

item.title: Govt takes measures for peaceful Durga Puja
item.description:
The government has directed the relevant ministries, administration and law enforcement agencies to take all necessary measures to ensure peaceful, festive and safe celebrations of the upcoming Durga Puja.
The authorities have also been asked to maintain communal harmony, prevent rumours and ensure prompt legal action through impartial investigations in the event of any untoward incident.
The directives were issued at an inter-ministerial preparatory meeting held at the Ministry of Religious Affairs on Tuesday morning. State Minister for Religious Affairs Mohammad Shamim Kaiser chaired the meeting.
The state minister said the government is committed to ensuring a safe and festive environment for Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of the Hindu community. He also stressed ensuring the proper distribution of grants allocated by the Prime Minister’s Office to Puja mandaps across the country through the Puja Welfare Trust.
Noting the increase in the number of Puja mandaps, he instructed local administrations and law enforcement agencies to remain vigilant and ensure proper management and security during idol immersion.
He called for continuing the longstanding practice of maintaining necessary silence during azan and prayer times to uphold social and religious harmony. He also urged people to refrain from making derogatory remarks about the deities of other religions.
The state minister directed authorities not to cover up any untoward incident but to conduct impartial investigations and take action against those responsible.
“We do not want to remain in the denial stage,” he said, stressing that no premature comments should be made about an offender’s identity or motive and that the facts should be established through investigation before taking action.
He also instructed authorities to promptly verify old or edited photos and videos used to spread rumours on social media. He called on intelligence agencies and law enforcement bodies to play an effective role in countering rumours and urged socially conscious young people to help disseminate accurate information.
He said public confidence in maintaining communal harmony would grow if swift investigations were followed by strict and exemplary punishment under the law for criminal offences.
Special Assistant to the Prime Minister (state minister rank) Bijon Kanti Sarker, Religious Affairs Secretary Munsi Alauddin Al Azad, representatives of various ministries and agencies, intelligence agencies, the Hindu Buddhist Christian Welfare Front, welfare trusts and Puja Celebration Council attended the meeting.

item.title: Woman dies of dengue at RMCH
item.description:
A 23-year-old woman has died of dengue at Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH), a day after a four-year-old child died of the disease at the same hospital.
The deceased, Farzana Khatun, hailed from Phulhari area of Shailkupa upazila in Jhenaidah. She died while undergoing treatment after developing dengue shock syndrome.
RMCH spokesperson Dr Shamim Ahmed confirmed the matter around 11am on Tuesday. He said Farzana was admitted to the hospital at 7am on Sunday. She died at 9:22am the following day while undergoing treatment.
He said 33 new dengue patients were admitted to RMCH in the past 24 hours, while 33 patients were discharged after receiving treatment. As of Tuesday, 110 dengue patients were undergoing treatment at the hospital.

item.title: Amit urges global firms to join Bangladesh offshore bidding round
item.description:
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit on Tuesday urged international oil and gas companies to participate in the Bangladesh Offshore Bidding Round 2026.
He made the call while addressing the Ministerial Address on the Strategic Stage of the two-day World Energies Summit in London, where he highlighted Bangladesh’s growing energy demand, offshore energy potential and improved investment framework.
The state minister also highlighted the government’s commitment to increasing the exploration and production of domestic gas and energy resources amid the country’s rapidly growing energy demand, according to a press release.
At the event, which will end on Wednesday, Bangladesh’s growing energy demand, offshore energy potential and improved investment framework were presented before international investors.
The state minister invited international oil and gas companies to participate in the Bangladesh Offshore Bidding Round 2026, under which a total of 26 blocks in the Bay of Bengal have been opened for investors, including 11 shallow-water blocks and 15 deep-water blocks.
Chairman of Invest Bangladesh Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun presented an overview of Bangladesh’s overall investment climate, highlighting macroeconomic stability, the growing momentum of investment and the government’s supportive policies for international investors.
The presentation also highlighted Bangladesh’s relatively unexplored offshore potential, availability of modern seismic data and the competitive commercial terms of the Offshore Model Production Sharing Contract 2026.
The Bangladesh delegation called upon international energy companies to review the geological and seismic data and directly contact the Bangladesh government and Bangladesh Oil, Gas & Mineral Corporation (Petrobangla) to participate in the ongoing bidding round.
On the first day of the summit, the Bangladesh delegation also held meetings with four international oil companies on the sidelines.
During the meetings, the delegation highlighted the benefits of the ongoing offshore bidding round and requested the companies to participate in the bidding process.
On the final day of the summit on Wednesday, meetings will be held with four more major companies from around the world.

item.title: Mir Shahe Alam: Local govt elections to begin in January, end by June 6
item.description:
State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam has said local government elections will begin in January and be completed by June 6.
He made the remarks while speaking to reporters after a meeting on law and order at the Rangpur Deputy Commissioner’s Office on Tuesday afternoon.
“According to the Election Commission, the local government elections will begin in January and continue until June 6. The law and order situation must be improved further to ensure smooth elections,” he said.
The state minister said the government is committed to holding the elections in a free, fair and impartial manner.
“Under the direct instructions of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, we will take all necessary measures to ensure free, fair and impartial elections,” he said.
“We want to assure the people and candidates that the government will not allow the elections to be tainted by irregularities or any other wrongdoing,” he added.
Mir Shahe Alam said Tk127 crore had been allocated over the past six months for road repairs and development in Rangpur.
He said the ministry had also sent a Tk3,600-crore project to the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) for infrastructure development in Rangpur, Lalmonirhat, Kurigram and Nilphamari.
Another Tk1,650-crore project for the Rangpur division, based on proposals from lawmakers, is awaiting ECNEC approval, he added. The state minister said new projects had also been taken up to improve public health and develop municipalities across the Rangpur division. The projects are currently in the pipeline.
“We will bring the entire country under balanced allocation and development under the instructions of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman,” he said.
On agricultural development, Mir Shahe Alam said the government plans to prioritise region-specific crops through a “zone map” and take necessary measures based on the crops predominantly grown in each area.
Regarding the Teesta Master Plan, he said the government was working on it and would move towards implementation soon. “The government is committed to implementing the Teesta plan,” he said.

item.title: Morocco's king appoints Marrakesh mayor El Mansouri as first woman prime minister
item.description:
The king of Morocco on Tuesday named Marrakesh mayor Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri the country's first woman prime minister, the royal cabinet announced, after her party won last week's parliamentary elections.
Her centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) had dominated the vote, winning 97 out of 395 seats in the House of Representatives – 31 more than the next closest competitor, although the poll was marked by the lowest turnout in two decades.
The royal cabinet said King Mohammed VI has now tasked the 50-year-old, who also served as housing minister, with "forming the new government".
Without an outright majority, the PAM will have to form a coalition with other parties for its five-year tenure, though the monarch retains broad powers over major policies.
The PAM was founded in 2008 by current royal adviser Fouad Ali El Himma as a counterweight to the country's Islamist movement.
El Mansouri was also the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh, winning the office in 2009 before losing it six years later, then retaking it again in 2021.
El Mansouri's cabinet will have to tackle several pressing issues including unemployment and living costs, as well as persistent social disparities particularly weighing on young people.
"Young people are going through a crisis and we must provide them with answers," she said during the campaign. "We want to restore their hope, not only through speeches, but through concrete solutions."
Her government will also be expected to make billions of dollars in investments linked to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, jointly organized with Spain and Portugal.
The parliamentary vote came just weeks after tens of thousands of mainly young Moroccan migrants rushed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, a crisis that highlighted socioeconomic frustrations among the youth.
It also came a year after a Gen-Z protest movement took to the streets to demand better health and education.
Her party has pledged average annual economic growth of five percent, inflation of two percent and the creation of at least one million new jobs over its five-year term.
The PAM was followed in the polls by the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which heads the outgoing coalition and won 66 seats.
The right-wing Istiqlal party came third with 65 seats, while the Islamist opposition's Justice and Development Party (PJD) took 54 seats.
The PJD made significant gains after winning just 13 seats in 2021, having focused its campaign in part on fighting corruption.
Its chief, former prime minister Abdelilah Benkirane, hailed a "victory" but ruled out joining a coalition led by the PAM, which he said was "tainted by fraud", without providing details.

A bird market takes place every Monday and Thursday at Dewanhat intersection in Chattogram city. Temporary stalls are set up beside the road and in nearby areas for a few hours from the afternoon. item.title: Questions raised over upper house; PM’s tenure should not be capped
item.description:
• According to a July Charter proposal, an individual could serve as prime minister for a maximum of 10 years

  • 30 political parties, including the BNP, had agreed to the proposal. Yesterday, however, an objection was raised against it

Representatives of television and online news outlets, as well as people who regularly attend talk-shows, have questioned whether there is a need for an upper house of parliament in a country such as Bangladesh.

Some also argued that it would be inappropriate to introduce a provision limiting an individual to a maximum of 10 years as prime minister.

The views were expressed on Tuesday at a consultation meeting between the parliamentary special committee on constitutional reform and representatives of television and online news outlets and talk-show commentators.

The meeting was held in the Cabinet Room of the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament).

Following the meeting, Special Committee Chairman and Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed briefed journalists at Parliament’s Media Centre on the discussions.

He said some participants had questioned whether a bicameral parliament was necessary at all in Bangladesh, given its unitary system of government. Some had proposed reconsidering the issue.

He further said there had been consensus in the July National Charter on establishing a bicameral parliament and that the special committee intended to proceed accordingly. If the proposals raised at the consultation were considered by the various parties in parliament, he said, they could be examined further.

One proposal in the July National Charter states that a provision would be introduced limiting an individual to a maximum of 10 years in office as prime minister. All 30 parties, including the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), had agreed to the proposal. At Tuesday’s consultation, however, some participants expressed opposition to it.

After the meeting, Salahuddin Ahmed also said some participants had described such a 10-year limit as undemocratic. The committee, however, said the proposal to set a 10-year limit had originally come from BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman. According to the committee, the proposal was made with the aim of preventing the establishment of an individual-based authoritarian system.

Salahuddin Ahmed said the BNP had not changed its position. He added that the matter could be discussed if the Opposition raised a proposal on it in parliament.

Asked whether there was scope for concessions on issues in the July National Charter on which the BNP holds a differing position, Salahuddin Ahmed said, “If the Opposition joins the discussions and seeks to depart from certain provisions of the July National Charter through dialogue, that too can be discussed. However, we intend to implement the July National Charter as it was formulated and signed. If the Opposition has anything to say on any particular issue, that can be addressed through consensus. But for that, they have to come to the discussions.”

According to sources at the consultation, proposals and suggestions were made on establishing a permanent framework for a caretaker government, ensuring the independence of the judiciary, creating a balance between the powers of the prime minister and the president, and involving the opposition in the process of amending the Constitution.

Speaking on the proposed upper house of parliament, some participants said the existing unicameral parliament had yet to become fully effective. They questioned how effective a bicameral legislature would be and said its establishment would also increase the state’s expenditure.

Special Committee Chairman Salahuddin Ahmed told journalists that the committee had yet to decide what form a caretaker government should take or who should be included in it. He said the July Charter contained differing views, or notes of dissent, on some aspects of the issue.

He said an open discussion was needed on how a caretaker government should be constituted and what form the government should take. Parliament would consider whichever proposal was deemed appropriate, he said.

The special committee chairman further said that some participants at the consultation had proposed changes to the Constitution’s preamble and to the fundamental principles of state policy. Participants were asked to submit their proposals in writing.

Among those attending the consultation were chorcha.com editor Sohrab Hassan, Bangla Vision Chief Editor Abdul Hai Siddique, Asian TV CEO Hasnain Khurshed, Jamuna Television CEO Fahim Ahmed, RTV Head of News Ilias Hossain and Dhaka Stream Editor-in-Chief Iftekhar Mahmud.

The talk-show commentators present included Shakhawat Hossain Sayantha, Abdun Noor Tushar and Sahed Alam.
